items.title: Alan Broadbent interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 26, 2023
items.q: That’s what I really — whatever I learned from Johnny Mandel and everybody else, now it began the time of refining my ear and where Mahler, say in a particular passage in the violins... So if I had to choose what — I always love many flutes in unison. And one of the most beautiful examples is in Mah

ctx.x: An Alanism, yes. That takes a lot of — a certain attitude, some restraint, and as you said there’s a craft in that as well, to be satisfied that you’ve added a small bit that makes the whole that much better.

That’s the point. That’s the point. And there are other projects I have where the producer or the artist just, “Go!” You know. And I go — appropriately so you know. Because I’m always moving: composer, arranger, you know I’m moved by the situation. I’m not trying to outdo it or anything. I always want to be a part of this song, create some kind of sub- song underneath it as I like to put it, so that I have another song going on, even with say © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Natalie Cole singing “Stardust” I have another “Stardust” going on, however subtley so I can add that way and to me it has a subliminal effect on people because we’re tuned to recognize things when we’re listening to them. So there’s a way of setting up those recognitions and orchestration, a little phrase or something. A person might not know because they’re only hearing this top line, but Alan under here is adding something, “Oh, what is that?” So that’s my goal is that in a standard song that I can pretend to…
